## What are we doing?

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

You can write using the Visual editor, or the Source script in [Markdown](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/lesson-1.html)

In this case, we want to create a simple dynamic report, but more complex webpages can be build (e.g. <https://ibartomeus.github.io/CropPollinationModels/>)

## Steps:

### Read data

We will use here as an example data from algal hervibores.

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
#| label: read data
#| echo: true
#| warning: false

d <- read.csv("data/Herbivore_specialisation.csv", row.names = 1)
#head(d)
n <- nrow(d)
```

Note that we want to show both the code and the output, so we tagged `echo: true`. The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed). We don't want to see any warning (`false`).

We can indicate that the data has `{r} n` columns. If you see this on html, note that I did call the last value from r directly. You can do this by typing {r} ts between ``` ``. ```

### Make some analysis

Next, we want to explore a bit the data. Choose your favorite analysis and play a bit.

```{r}
#| label: a simple plot
#| echo: true

#head(d)
boxplot(d$abundance ~ d$DayNight, las = 1, xlab = "Day / Night", ylab = "Abundance")
```

There is an (untested) lack of differences between day and night samplings.
